opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic problem is that once a benchmark is saturated, it stops telling you anything. If every frontier model scores ninety-something percent, you can't distinguish between them anymore, and you definitely can't tell whether the next model is meaningfully better. The remaining errors are often label noise or ambiguous questions rather than real capability gaps, so you end up arguing over a point or two that doesn't reflect anything about the model.

There's also a deeper issue. A lot of the classic benchmarks were designed when models were much weaker. They test things like multiple-choice knowledge recall or short, self-contained problems. That was a great signal a few years ago, but it's not what we actually care about now. Now we want to know whether a model can do economically valuable work: can it write a legal brief, debug a real codebase, put together a financial analysis, carry a long multi-step task to completion. A saturated multiple-choice test just isn't measuring that.

And then there's contamination and overfitting. Once a benchmark has been public and heavily used for a while, the questions or close variants of them leak into training data, and the whole field implicitly optimizes toward it. So high scores can partly reflect familiarity with the test rather than general ability.

So for me, the takeaway is that evals need to keep moving with the models. We have to build harder, more realistic evaluations that are grounded in the tasks people actually do, ideally ones graded by real experts, so there's plenty of headroom and the numbers map onto something people care about in the real world. That's the only way to keep measuring progress rather than just confirming that the old tests are solved.

r001.rationale: The response says that when every frontier model scores in the ninety-something-percent range, the benchmark can no longer distinguish between them or show whether one is meaningfully better.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that a benchmark is really a measuring instrument, and once a model is scoring in the high nineties on something, the instrument basically stops telling you anything. If the top models are all clustered at 95, 97, 98 percent, the remaining gap between them is often just noise. It's label errors in the dataset, it's ambiguous questions, it's formatting quirks in how the answer gets parsed. So a one-point difference there doesn't actually reflect a meaningful difference in capability, and you can't use it to tell whether your next model is really better.

The other piece is that saturation usually means the benchmark no longer sits at the frontier of what's hard. When we first put out something like MMLU-style evals or the early math benchmarks, they were genuinely difficult, and the score tracked something real about reasoning or knowledge. But the field moves fast, the models get trained on data that looks more and more like the test, and pretty soon the eval is measuring "can you do this well-trodden task" rather than "can you do the thing we actually care about." And often the thing we care about has shifted, like can the model do multi-hour agentic work, or can it make real progress on an open research problem, not can it answer a multiple-choice question.

So what I find more useful is building evals where there's still a lot of headroom, where humans who are experts still clearly beat the models, because then the trend line over successive model generations is informative. You can watch the score go from five percent to twenty to forty and that actually tells you a story about progress. Once it's at ninety-eight, the story's over and you need a new benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response says that when models score in the high nineties, the benchmark stops being informative and small score gaps do not reflect meaningful capability differences.

astra-6.text:
Once a benchmark is saturated, it stops giving you much signal about what’s improving. If every model is getting close to 100%, you can’t really distinguish their capabilities, and a small difference in scores may not translate into a meaningful difference for users.

What you want is an evaluation that still exposes failures. Where does the model get stuck? What tasks can it complete reliably, and where does a person still need to step in? A saturated benchmark can still be useful as a regression check, but to measure progress, you need harder evaluations that reflect the things people actually want models to do.

r001.rationale: The response says that when every model is near 100%, the benchmark cannot really distinguish their capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
Once a benchmark is saturated, it stops helping you distinguish between models. If every model gets close to 100 percent, you can have meaningful improvements in capability that barely move the score. And a high score can look like we’ve solved a whole category of problems, when we’ve really just solved the particular tasks that benchmark captures.

What I want from an evaluation is a way to see where models still struggle. Can they handle a harder problem, generalize to a new situation, or complete a task reliably? Benchmarks with room for improvement give us a much clearer signal about that progress.

r001.rationale: The response says that when every model scores close to 100%, the benchmark stops distinguishing them and may barely reflect meaningful capability improvements.
